evidence.claim: Georgetown Pike runs 11.79 miles from Dranesville to Langley, passing through Great Falls and along the edge of Great Falls Park.
evidence.quote: Known as Georgetown Pike, the state highway runs 11.79 mi (18.97 km) from SR 7 in Dranesville east to SR 123 in Langley.

evidence.claim: Built between 1813 and 1827, the pike had a crowned stone roadbed.
evidence.quote: as built in 1813–1827. A crowned and graduated stone highway

evidence.claim: Workers used hand tools and horse-drawn equipment to clear, blast and fill the rough terrain, adding retaining walls, culverts and bridges where needed.
evidence.quote: Men using hand tools and horse-drawn equipment formed the roadbed, clearing, blasting, plowing, scooping, and filling the rough terrain. Stone retaining walls, culverts, arches, and bridges were built where necessary

evidence.claim: In 1820, Falls Bridge Turnpike Company president John Mason Jr. reported large fitted stones twelve inches deep at the center, topped with six inches of broken stone.
evidence.quote: John Mason, Jr., president of the Falls Bridge Turnpike Company, wrote to the Board of Public Works in 1820 that the roadbed was "paved with large stone, closely fitted together, 12 inches deep in the centre, falling off to 6 inches on the sides, and covered with broken stone 6 inches deep from side to side;

evidence.claim: The original route continued to the Potomac at Chain Bridge, beyond today’s SR 193.
evidence.quote: When first constructed, the Georgetown Pike continued through the District of Columbia's Alexandria County (now Arlington County, Virginia) to the banks of the Potomac.

evidence.quote: In 1963, Virginia completed the Dolley Madison Boulevard bypass in the McLean area, as an alternative to widening both the existing Chain Bridge Road and Georgetown Pike.

evidence.claim: Great Falls was once known unofficially as Forestville, but another Forestville already had a post office.
evidence.quote: Early on, the village was known as Forestville (unofficially, since there was already a Forestville with a Post Office)

evidence.quote: but was renamed Great Falls in 1955.

evidence.claim: from the nearby falls of the Potomac.
evidence.quote: It is named for the nearby Great Falls of the Potomac River.

evidence.claim: Forestville survives in the name of the old school, built in 1889 and enlarged in 1911 by adding the Floris School.
evidence.quote: The Forestville School was built in 1889 as a one-room school, and expanded in 1911 with the appendage of the Floris School.

evidence.claim: After closing as a school in 1922, the building became a residence and later the Great Falls Post Office, from 1959 to 1982.
evidence.quote: After closing as a school in 1922, it served as a residence and then as the Great Falls Post Office from 1959 until 1982.

evidence.claim: The resulting L-shaped wooden building has weatherboard siding and a metal cross-gable roof.
evidence.quote: It is an L-shaped wood-frame structure covered in weatherboards and topped by a standing-seam metal cross-gable roof.

evidence.quote: The Great Falls Grange Hall was built in 1929, and is a 1+1⁄2-story brick building with a gable front. It features a front porch supported by concrete pillars

evidence.claim: Great Falls Park preserves remnants of the Patowmack Canal and the canal town of Matildaville beside the Potomac.
evidence.quote: Remnants of the canal and of a village around the canal named Matildaville are still visible in the park.

evidence.claim: The canal was designed to carry boats past the river’s rapids.
evidence.quote: a series of five inoperative canals located in Maryland and Virginia, United States, that was designed to bypass rapids in the Potomac River

evidence.claim: At Great Falls, workers included enslaved people rented from nearby plantations, indentured servants and other laborers.
evidence.quote: Crews consisted of unskilled laborers, skilled indentured servants, and slaves rented from nearby plantations.

evidence.claim: They used black powder to cut through rock for the final three locks.
evidence.quote: With one of the earliest uses in this country of black-powder blasting, workers forced a channel through the rock cliffs for the final three locks.

evidence.claim: High construction costs and insufficient revenue bankrupted the company.
evidence.quote: High construction costs, particularly at the Great Falls section, and insufficient revenues bankrupted the company.

evidence.claim: Viewing platforms in the park overlook the falls; the canal remains tell a separate story of attempts to navigate them.
evidence.quote: The park has several viewing platforms that provide visitors with vantage points overlooking the falls.

evidence.claim: The National Park Service took over Great Falls Park in 1966.
evidence.quote: Great Falls Park was a part of the Northern Virginia Parks system until it was transferred to the NPS in 1966.

evidence.claim: Georgetown Pike descends through sharp curves into Difficult Run’s valley.
evidence.quote: The state highway features many sharp curves as it drops into the stream valley of Difficult Run.

evidence.claim: The stream’s name came from long-boatmen working in the Patowmack Company era, who found two bends of the Potomac near its mouth treacherous.
evidence.quote: It was named by long-boatmen in the time of the Patowmack Company, who found the two sharp bends of the Potomac near Difficult Run's mouth treacherous.

evidence.claim: Road builders faced their own crossing here: John Templeman designed and built a chain bridge to carry the pike over the stream.
evidence.quote: He designed and built an additional chain bridge to carry the Pike over Difficult Run.

evidence.quote: John Templeman, builder of the Potomac Chain Bridge in 1808, served as superintendent of the road from December 1, 1817, to April 30, 1818.

flags: No official designating-agency or tourism page is cached. Scenic designation and drive description rely on the SR 193 article; no agency rationale beyond scenic value or journey time is available.

Retained all current moments. Dropped the promise of hearing the falls and the absolute claim that the Potomac is never visible: the cache ties these observations to the longer historic alignment and its National Register description.
Bull Neck Run is intentionally short: the cache provides no bridge date, public stopping place, or verified viewing access. No notice or coordinates were added.
The Difficult Run article incorrectly conflates the 1974 byway designation with becoming a state highway. Used SR 193 for designation history.
Canal articles disagree on opening and abandonment dates; omitted those dates. Great Falls Park is a separate excursion, inserted between the village and Difficult Run.
